evidence_quotes.quote: only 316 localities have some kind of sewage collection and/or treatment system, which is equivalent to 13% of the total. These localities benefit 620,617 people, that is, 27% of the rural population with access to drinking water.
we used as a proxy the percentage of households with household sewage connections with respect to the total with potable water, which allowed us to approximate the effective coverage of the service

In Chile, access to rural sanitation is regulated by Law No. 20.998 regarding Rural Sanitation Services (SSR), in force since November 2020. This regulation recognizes social organizations - non-profit committees and cooperatives - as the operators of rural sanitation services, authorized to manage drinking water and sanitation within a defined service area, usually associated with a locality.

Consequently, any increase in regulatory obligations - for example, higher effluent quality control requirements - has a direct impact on their operating costs and must be financed through tariffs, with potential impact on their economic viability.

Although Law No. 20.998 requires the formal registration of operators to access licenses, by the end of 2023 most of them were not formalized. In 2024, 2,291 of the 2,241 rural health services currently recognized by the MOP were registered (93.86%).

Subsequently, between May 2024 and March 2025, a national survey of technical data was carried out to characterize the state of implementation, operation and coverage of existing systems, with their systematization and validation.

As of March 2025, only 27% of the systems analyzed show adequate performance, while the remaining 73% show structural or operational failures, or lack sufficient information to be evaluated. Of this total, around 30% of the SRHs are in a critical state, requiring urgent intervention.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural community and household sanitation service access in Chile across 2,441 recognized Rural Sanitation Services (SSRs), measuring locality-level wastewater collection and treatment availability, relative household sewage connection coverage (start-ups), benefited population, user tariffs, and system operational continuity.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain reading: Yes — examines Law No. 20.998, Supreme Decree No. 50, Supreme Decrees No. 90/2000 and 46/2002, SEIA permitting thresholds, multi-agency institutional fragmentation, operator formalization, tariffs, and management models. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes (borderline on causal isolation, as Section 3 also emphasizes technical and geographic factors) — examines concrete rule-type mechanisms governing rural sanitation provision and access, including: (1) regulatory structure and operator registration/licensing rules under Law No. 20.998 and Article 106 of Regulation No. 50 (segmenting utilities into major, medium, and minor regulatory tiers and requiring registry enrollment to access licenses and state investment, empirically cross-tabulated with coverage and critical failures); (2) utility ownership/management structure (44% municipal operation vs. 41% subsidized non-profit committees/cooperatives vs. 13% unknown); and (3) statutory cost-recovery tariff rules under Law No. 20.998 interacting with uniform effluent monitoring mandates (DS 90/2000 and DS 46/2002), showing empirically how monthly user fees (US$3.41-US$7.76) and compliance costs strain financial viability, compliance (96.3% unmonitored), and operational sustainability.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical evidence from a national administrative and field-validated technical survey conducted between May 2024 and March 2025, integrating 2017-2023 internal SSSR regional files and the June 2024 Official SSSR Cadaster across all 16 regions of Chile (2,441 SSRs and 326 rural sanitation systems). Lack of regression effect sizes does not preclude systematic-review inclusion per Criterion 6.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports sanitation access, connection, affordability/tariff, and reliability/continuity outcomes: 13% (316/2,441) of SSRs have sewage collection or treatment benefiting 620,617 people (27% of rural population with drinking water); 53% relative household sewage connection coverage across networked SSRs; monthly user fees of US$3.41 to US$7.76; and operational status (27% adequate, 73% with structural/operational failures, 30% in critical condition, and 20 networked systems discharging untreated wastewater).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (2,441 recognized SSR operators and 326 rural sanitation systems in 316 localities serving rural inhabitants in Chile), exposure (Law No. 20.998 regulatory tiers, registration/licensing and cost-recovery tariff rules, utility management models, and uniform DS 90/DS 46 compliance standards), outcome (coverage, household sewer connections, tariffs, compliance, and operational failure), and study design (cross-sectional national administrative cadaster and technical-operational survey) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional descriptive empirical study using a consolidated national administrative cadaster and field-validated technical-operational survey (2017-2025 records integrated in 2024-2025), combined with regulatory and institutional analysis
population_and_sample: 2,441 officially recognized Rural Sanitation Services serving 2,308,071 rural drinking-water inhabitants across all 16 regions (3 macrozones) of Chile, including 326 rural wastewater collection/treatment systems in 316 localities (units of analysis: rural sanitation service/system and locality, with aggregated household connection and population counts)
exposure: Regulatory and governance mechanisms governing rural sanitation in Chile under Law No. 20.998 and Regulation No. 50 (mandatory operator registration and licensing, Article 106 three-tier regulatory segmentation into major/medium/minor services, statutory cost-recovery tariff rules, and municipal vs. subsidized non-profit community committee management models), alongside uniform environmental discharge and monitoring regulations (Supreme Decrees No. 90/2000 and No. 46/2002, SEIA thresholds)
outcome: Locality wastewater collection and treatment coverage (316 of 2,441 SSRs, 13%, serving 620,617 people), relative household sewage connection coverage (53% across networked SSRs), monthly user fees (US$3.41-US$7.76), effluent monitoring compliance (3.7% quarterly or more frequent; 69.5% none), and operational continuity/failure (27% adequate, 73% structural/operational failures, 30% critical, 20 networked systems discharging without treatment)
rationale: Full-text empirical study examining rural sanitation coverage, household sewage connection coverage, user tariffs, and operational sustainability across Chile's 2,441 recognized Rural Sanitation Services (326 sanitation systems) using a newly consolidated and field-validated national administrative database (2024-2025). Satisfies c1 and c4 by reporting locality sanitation availability, household sewage connection rates, monthly fees, and system failure/abandonment. Satisfies c2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification because it analyzes Law No. 20.998 operator registration/licensing requirements, Article 106 regulatory segmentation, municipal vs. community-committee utility ownership/management models, and statutory cost-recovery tariff rules interacting with uniform DS 90/2000 and DS 46/2002 compliance burdens. Confidence is set to medium because the quantitative tables are descriptive cross-tabulations (without multivariable effect estimates, which is a meta-analysis gate rather than a review-inclusion gate per Criterion 6) and share focus with technological and geographic factors.
